title: Effects of Aquaculture Ponds on Groundwater Salinization and Submarine Groundwater Discharge in Tidally Influenced Coastal Aquifers
content:
Abstract

Coastal aquaculture ponds store saline, nutrient-rich water and can leak into adjacent aquifers, yet their impacts on groundwater salinization and submarine groundwater discharge (SGD) under tidal conditions remain poorly quantified. We use a two-dimensional variable density groundwater flow and solute transport model to examine how a leaking saline pond interacts with a tidally influenced coastal aquifer. The model tracks the evolution of a pond infiltrated saline plume (ISP) and its interactions with the upper saline plume (USP) and saltwater wedge (SW) for a suite of scenarios spanning tidal amplitude, beach slope, hydraulic conductivity, inland freshwater head, pond water salinity, and pond configuration. We evaluate metrics of salinized areas, SGD partitioning, mixing between ISP, USP and SW and associated changes in saltwater residence times. Results show that pond salinity is the primary control on overall salinization and SGD partitioning, while pond water level and compacted-soil permeability control how strongly pond leakage perturbs the USP and SW. The presence of the pond generally reduces USP extent and USP-derived saline SGD, while the SW response depends on pond salinity, changing from slight expansion at low salinity to contraction at high salinity. Importantly, pond-derived saline water typically overlaps with about 80 percent of the USP area (median across all simulations) and causes reduced saltwater residence times in the USP. These interactions imply that coastal aquaculture ponds can intensify groundwater salinization and reorganize tidally driven saltwater circulation, with important implications for how aquaculture-derived solutes are transformed and exported to nearshore marine ecosystems via SGD pathways.
